title: Bales, bins, and what a yard buys
description: Follow the bottle from a household pile to a pressed bale.

questions.question: This close-up is crushed bottles pressed into a block. What is for sale?
options: A volume of one clean grade, ready to travel
Rubbish the yard pays to remove
New bottles already filled
Glass, once labels fall off
questions.answer: A volume of one clean grade, ready to travel
questions.explanation: A bale is the product. One bottle is not a sale. A sorted pile is how a bale begins.

questions.question: Bottles sit gathered in open bags. What still has to happen before they are a bale?
options: Keep the grade together, dry, and drop the strangers
Add film so the bags look full
Hose them until they stay wet
Mix in jerry cans for weight
questions.answer: Keep the grade together, dry, and drop the strangers
questions.explanation: Gathered is not finished. Grade, dry, no extras.

questions.question: A marked bin stands ready. What is the bin for?
options: One stream — not a second home for mixed leftovers
Anything plastic, including oil cans and chargers
Only glass
Only film
questions.answer: One stream — not a second home for mixed leftovers
questions.explanation: A recycling bin is a promise of a stream. Mixing breaks the promise.

questions.question: Coloured bins stand in a row. What is the row teaching?
options: Different materials get different homes
Colour is decoration
All bins take the same mixed bag
The green bin is for garden soil only, always
questions.explanation: The row is a sort you can see. One bag into every bin is the old mistake.

questions.question: A wall of stacked PET bales sits in a yard. Who is the customer?
options: A reprocessor who buys one grade at a time
A shopper buying drinks
A landfill that pays for colour
A glass factory
questions.answer: A reprocessor who buys one grade at a time
questions.explanation: The stack is inventory. The customer wants PET, not a surprise can.

questions.question: A mixed waste pile, no grades visible. What would make it a product?
options: Pulling one grade out and keeping it clean
Photographing it from farther away
Adding water
Tying the whole pile in one liner
questions.answer: Pulling one grade out and keeping it clean
questions.explanation: A pile is not a grade. Hands make the product.

questions.question: Beach crates and debris, far from a Kenyan kiosk. How did household plastic get this far?
options: Wind and water move what leaves a drain
Crates grow on beaches
Only ships drop plastic; houses cannot
Sand manufactures bottles
questions.answer: Wind and water move what leaves a drain
questions.explanation: A coast is often the last mile of an inland habit.

questions.question: A beach of mixed fragments. What is already lost as a sale?
options: Grade identity — broken mixed pieces are hard to buy as one product
Nothing — fragments sell better than bottles
Only the sand is lost
Colour, because the sun bleaches value back
questions.answer: Grade identity — broken mixed pieces are hard to buy as one product
questions.explanation: Catch it whole and dry. Fragments on a beach are usually past the sale.

questions.question: Caps in one pile, bottles somewhere else. If you photograph proof, what is honest?
options: Caps as their own grade, or bottles without caps — not a sealed jumble
Every bottle still tightly capped to look unused
Caps hidden under bottles
One cap and one can and one bag in one frame
questions.answer: Caps as their own grade, or bottles without caps — not a sealed jumble
questions.explanation: The photo is a sample of a product. Show the sort you actually did.

questions.question: HDPE jugs of many household shapes. What do they share?
options: A family — kitchen jugs and cans, not PET water bottles
They are all grade 1 PET
They are all film
They are all glass
questions.answer: A family — kitchen jugs and cans, not PET water bottles
questions.explanation: Shape varies. The family is HDPE. PET crackles; these thud.
